source: Ismayilzada et al. (2026) Large Language Models Align with the Human Brain during Creative Thinking
finding: LLM hidden states were compared with human fMRI during the Alternate Uses Task. Bigger models align more with the default mode network (DMN), but not on a non-creative control task.
numbers: Human data: Beaty 2018, 170 subjects, 46 AUT stimuli. 24 models, 270M to 72B. DMN alignment vs size at prompt stage r=0.55 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.77), Spearman 0.65. Same test on non-creative object-characteristics task r=0.09 (p=0.66).
limits: Correlational. Alignment is a representational similarity, not a mechanism. Models have no prefrontal control system.
agent_relevance: Idea-space alignment grows with scale; control is not what scale buys. Free association is cheap, control is the scarce part.

source: Ismayilzada et al. (2026) Large Language Models Align with the Human Brain during Creative Thinking (time course and networks)
finding: Alignment with originality is clearest while the model reads the prompt and fades once it generates a response. Frontoparietal (control) alignment with originality is weaker and not significant after correction.
numbers: AUT score vs DMN alignment r=0.52 (CI 0.07 to 0.76). FPN r=0.46 (CI -0.06 to 0.77, corrected p=0.079). DMN minus somatomotor control median +0.15 at prompt stage (18 of 23 models, p=0.002); no difference at response stage (p=0.94, 0.34). Gemma-3 within-family size r=0.90; Qwen2.5 r=0.89.
limits: Few models (23 to 24). Peak layer depends on pooling method. Temperature 0.7, 1024 tokens.
agent_relevance: Generation looks less brain-like than reading. Put the novelty push at framing time (O4 before generating).

source: Ismayilzada et al. (2026) Large Language Models Align with the Human Brain during Creative Thinking (post-training)
finding: A creativity-tuned Llama-3.1-8B kept alignment with high-creativity brain responses and lost alignment with low-creativity ones. A reasoning-distilled variant showed negative alignment with high-creativity responses.
numbers: CrPO-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-cre: positive for high, none for low. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B: negative for high. Exact values only in Fig 4 (not read).
limits: Negative reasoning effect does not appear in the Qwen counterpart. Variants differ in data and length, so no causal claim.
agent_relevance: Reasoning training may push away from the creative pattern. Do not assume longer reasoning helps idea generation.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Strong Memory, Weak Control: executive functioning in LLMs
finding: LLMs beat human norms on working memory but are weak on attention control and flexibility. Working memory did not predict executive scores.
numbers: 6 instruction-tuned models (Gemma-2 9B/27B, Llama-3.1 8B/70B, Qwen2 7B/72B), 30 prompt variants each. Backward digit span length 15: 0.00 to 0.83 vs human about 0. Parameter count vs span r=0.82 (p<0.05). No human-like WM to executive correlation.
quote: LLMs may have deficits in attentional control and cognitive flexibility
limits: Behaviour only. Models of 27B or more were 4-bit quantised. Only 6 plus 3 reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Memory is cheap, control is scarce. A scaffold must supply control (inhibit, shift) from outside the model.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Strong Memory, Weak Control (WCST and Flanker)
finding: On the Wisconsin Card Sorting Task models score far below healthy adults, with more perseveration. Flanker incongruent accuracy is low too.
numbers: WCST accuracy 0.29 to 0.53 (3,060 trials per model) vs 0.77 humans. Perseverative errors 0.20 to 0.33 vs 0.12. Flanker incongruent about 40 to 60% vs 93 to 96% humans. WCST accuracy falls with dialogue length, r -0.28 to -0.51 (all p<0.05).
limits: Instruction-tuned open models only. Human numbers are published norms, not a matched sample.
agent_relevance: Context length hurts set shifting. Reset context between tries (fits our fresh-start operators).

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Strong Memory, Weak Control (reasoning models)
finding: Reasoning mode fixes Flanker but not card sorting. Thought strings often failed to finish in 30,000 tokens on WCST.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B incongruent 0.471 to 0.910 with reasoning. Qwen2-32B 0.638 to 0.985. WCST: reasoning models did not beat non-reasoning ones, even with strategy hints. Backward span only helped weak baselines.
limits: Reasoning model list differs across sections of the paper. No exact WCST figures.
agent_relevance: Reasoning helps suppress a surface cue, not switch rules. Add an external set-shift trigger, not just more thinking.

source: Visual LLMs exhibit human-level cognitive flexibility in the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (2025)
finding: With chain-of-thought and text input, three frontier models match or beat humans on card sorting. Without CoT they fail.
numbers: WCST-64, 10 runs per condition. Standardised categories completed: Claude-3.5 Sonnet 0.02 (standard, visual) vs 1.00 (CoT, text); Gemini-1.5 Pro 0.08 vs 0.96; GPT-4o 0.06 vs 0.92. Humans (N=30) 4.73 of 5 categories. Perseverative errors CoT text: Claude 6.30, Gemini 6.80, GPT-4o 7.60, humans 6.87.
limits: No significance tests. Visual input worse (GPT-4o card-count accuracy 0%). Author names not read.
agent_relevance: The scaffold moves flexibility from near 0 to near 1: strong support for making the rule hypothesis explicit and revisable.

source: Visual LLMs ... WCST (2025), ablations
finding: Removing the told rule exclusivity hurts; simulated inhibitory-control impairment hurts sharply.
numbers: Without rule exclusivity, CoT text categories: Gemini 4.8 to 2.6, GPT-4o 4.6 to 3.5, Claude 5.0 to 4.7. Role-played inhibitory impairment: Gemini 4.80 to 1.70, Claude 5.00 to 1.50.
limits: Role-played impairment may copy stereotypes, not mechanism. Small n.
agent_relevance: Models flex when rules are explicit; ambiguous real tasks are harder. Make the candidate rule set explicit.

source: Patel, Wang & Fan (2026) Deficient executive control in transformer attention (press report)
finding: Stroop accuracy of frontier models collapses as list length grows, while humans keep control.
numbers: Incongruent colour naming: GPT-4o 91% at 5 words, 1% at 20 and 40 words. Claude 3.5 Sonnet fell to 10% at 40 words. Lists 1 to 40 words.
limits: Press page only; the PNAS Nexus paper was not opened. Other press mentions of newer models not verified. Authors call CoT or code shortcuts avoidance.
agent_relevance: Inhibition fails with load; keep interference sets short and have code, not the model, enforce suppression.

source: Machine Psychophysics: Cognitive Control in Vision-Language Models (2025)
finding: 108 vision-language models show congruency effects on Stroop and Flanker. A harder squared conflict (stimulus and response conflict) breaks even the largest models.
numbers: Stroop 84 trials; Flanker letter and number 180 each; congruency t=17.88 (letter), 16.85 (number), 8.99 (Stroop). Squared tasks: large models high on fully congruent but below chance on fully incongruent. No model near ceiling on both.
limits: Stimulus conflict only; synthetic stimuli; no prompting or CoT analysis; qualitative human comparison.
agent_relevance: Scaling alone does not give control. Do not assume a bigger model suppresses a dominant habit.

source: Cognitive Science preprint (GPT-4o executive function tasks), found by search
finding: Search summary: GPT-4o matched humans on Stroop interference, working memory updating and number switching, but diverged on Go/No-Go response inhibition and time-dependent control.
numbers: Not read; no numbers verified (page returned 404).
limits: Snippet only. Unverified.
agent_relevance: If true, inhibition is task-specific, so test our own loop on the exact control step it needs.

source: ExProf-Bench (executive function benchmark), found by search
finding: Search summary: benchmark built on the Miyake inhibition, shifting, updating model. Reports a jagged frontier where larger models do not reliably win on separable executive dimensions.
numbers: Not read; host unreachable.
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: Control skills are separable; measure each separately before relying on any.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2025) Divergent Creativity in Humans and Large Language Models
finding: On the Divergent Association Task (DAT), GPT-4 beat the human mean, Gemini Pro matched it, and newer models do not always do better. The most creative humans still beat every model tested.
numbers: Human sample about 100,000. GPT-4 above human mean (significant). GPT-4-turbo worse than GPT-4; 'ocean' in over 90% of its word sets; GPT-4 used 'microscope' in 70%. Top-decile humans above all models (releases Jan 2023 to Jun 2025).
limits: DAT measures word distance, not useful creativity. Heavy word repetition inside models.
agent_relevance: The ceiling is expert humans. Average novelty is cheap; the top tail needs more than loosening.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2025) Divergent Creativity (temperature)
finding: Raising GPT-4 temperature raised DAT scores and reduced word repetition.
numbers: Temperatures 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, n=500 generations each. Mean at highest temperature 85.6, higher than 72% of human scores.
limits: Only GPT-4, original DAT prompt. Higher temperature costs stability.
agent_relevance: Sampling noise is a crude, untargeted loosening dial, like random hypofrontality.

source: Bellemare-Pepin et al. (2025) Divergent Creativity (strategy prompts)
finding: Telling the model a strategy for the DAT changed scores. A varying-etymology strategy beat the plain prompt for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
numbers: Strategies: meaning opposition, thesaurus, etymology. All mean differences significant except thesaurus vs basic instruction. Exact means in Fig 5 (not read).
limits: Two models. Effect size not extracted.
agent_relevance: A named search strategy is a controlled way to relax control: the program picks the strategy, the model fills it in (O4).

source: Chen & Ding (2023) Probing the Creativity of LLMs: divergent semantic association (EMNLP Findings)
finding: On the DAT, greedy GPT-4 beats 96% of humans and GPT-3.5-turbo beats the average human. Sampling and temperature raise scores for models other than GPT-4, with a stability trade-off.
numbers: 96% (GPT-4 greedy). Abstract page only.
limits: Abstract only; prompts and tables not read. Bellemare-Pepin found weaker GPT-4 ranks with other prompts, so figures depend on setup.
agent_relevance: Early reference point for the DAT claim.

source: Peeperkorn et al. (2024) Is Temperature the Creativity Parameter of LLMs?
finding: Temperature has only a weak effect on novelty and reduces coherence. Not a creativity dial.
numbers: Llama 2-Chat 70B, 7 temperatures 0.001 to 2.0, 100 stories each, 36 raters, 31 stories. Novelty beta=.308 (p<.05, conditional R2=.385); coherence beta=.240 (p<.05, R2=.646). Typicality and cohesion not significant. Rater alpha .639.
limits: One model, one prompt, small human study, below-threshold agreement.
agent_relevance: Blunt loosening buys little novelty at real cost: argues for targeted loosening over temperature.

source: Nath, Dayan & Stevenson (2024) Characterising the Creative Process in Humans and LLMs
finding: Humans reach creative scores by either deep search (persistent) or broad jumping (flexible). LLMs lean one way per task, and for LLMs the flexible style scored higher.
numbers: 8 LLMs, 440 sequences (5 samples x 11 temperatures); 220 human students. LLM originality higher in flexible cluster (p<0.01) and above humans (p<0.001). Humans: no difference between clusters (p>0.05). Test-retest of jump count r=0.42 humans vs 0.22 LLMs.
limits: No correlation coefficients. Basic prompt, one embedding model, AUT may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Models need a forced flexible path; humans can succeed by persistence. Tracking jumps between semantic categories is a cheap program-side signal.

source: Nath et al. (2024) (temperature and prompt)
finding: Temperature did not change which path (persistent or flexible) a model took on the AUT.
numbers: Temperature effect on jumps and cluster on AUT p>0.05; on verbal fluency it affected jumps p<0.001, not cluster. Repetition penalty did not help.
limits: Same limits as above.
agent_relevance: Path style is prompt and model driven, not sampling driven. Change the frame to shift it.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) CreativityNeuro: steering model weights for divergent thinking
finding: A data-free weight perturbation on creativity-relevant parameters raised DAT scores and transferred to human-rated AUT and a Task Task. It beat prompting and sampling baselines.
numbers: 6 open models (3B to 14B). DAT up to +14 human percentile points (human reference N=9,297). CN 94.1 average percentile vs activation steering 93.9; prompt-only activation steering 87.8, prompting 87.9. Human eval N=720 on AUT and Task Task.
limits: Divergent thinking is a measure of creative potential, not creativity. Only a CAA-style steering baseline. Preprint.
agent_relevance: A loosen knob exists in weights, but a scaffold cannot use it. Prompting alone reached about the 88th percentile.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) CreativityNeuro (mode collapse)
finding: Baseline models collapse onto the same words, and CN reduces that.
numbers: Baseline: 25.5% of tokens in each model's top-10 words; galaxy, quasar, xylophone in the top 30 of all three families. CN cut top-10 share by 10.2 points and raised entropy by 0.59 nats (+10%).
limits: DAT vocabulary only; AUT and Task Task used embedding similarity.
agent_relevance: A program-side banlist of repeated ideas (our overlap check) targets the same collapse.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026) CreativityNeuro (entanglement)
finding: Making the model more divergent also hurt factual accuracy, and shielding fact weights did not protect it. Divergence and reasoning seem entangled in weights.
numbers: MMLU 5-shot, 500 questions, 5 seeds. Default masks -3.13 points; MMLU-protected masks a further -0.71 points while DAT +1.33 percentile.
limits: May be an artifact of the Wanda-style importance score. Authors say generation and selection should be separated.
agent_relevance: Supports separate generate and evaluate calls, not one loosened model doing both.

source: Olson et al. (2024) Steering Large Language Models to Evaluate and Amplify Creativity
finding: A creativity direction in Llama3-8B activations, found from 500 creative vs uncreative prompt pairs, steers stories and scores creativity.
numbers: Layer 8, strength 3, temperature 1.0. Llama3-70B judge agrees with one human annotator over 70% on pairwise creativity. Llama3-8B rates its own stories near 7 out of 9, a poor judge.
limits: One model, one dataset, one annotator, hand-picked layer. No coefficients in text.
agent_relevance: Small self-judges are not usable for the evaluate step; keep scoring external.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: open-ended homogeneity of language models
finding: Open-ended outputs are repetitive within a model and alike across models. Models and judges are poorly calibrated on answers that people rate differently.
numbers: Infinity-Chat: 26K queries, 6 categories, 17 subcategories, 31,250 human annotations (25 per item). Similarity figures not on the page read.
limits: Abstract page only.
agent_relevance: One model sampled many times gives correlated ideas: use different frames, not more samples.

source: Webb, Mondal & Momennejad (2025) Improving planning with LLMs: modular agentic architecture (MAP), Nature Communications
finding: A prefrontal-inspired set of LLM modules (monitor, predictor, evaluator, decomposer, orchestrator) lifts planning. The conflict Monitor is the most important part.
numbers: Tower of Hanoi 3 disks: about 7x zero-shot solved; best of 5 runs 100%; 4-disk OOD: baselines near 0%, MAP no invalid moves. Removing Monitor: 31% invalid moves vs 0%. PlanBench Logistics 24 vs CoT 17; Mystery BW 27.4 vs 10.6. StrategyQA 87.7 vs CoT 84.7 (human 87.0).
limits: GPT-4 for all modules; Llama3-70B version weaker. Task-specific prompts. Many calls.
agent_relevance: Direct agent-loop use of conflict monitoring. A separate monitor call is the machine counterpart of prefrontal control: it checks, it does not create.

source: Beaty et al. (2015) Default and executive network coupling supports creative idea production
finding: During idea generation the default network couples with right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, first via insula (salience), later via executive regions. Both networks work together.
numbers: N=25 (3 of 28 excluded), 46 trials, 12 s each. Global efficiency vs creativity r=.44, p=.02. Resting-state check n=42. Rater alpha .87.
limits: Small N, one task, responses not recorded in scanner, voxelwise p<.001 uncorrected for part of analysis.
agent_relevance: Control is not just switched off; it joins later. Fits a two-phase loop: loose first, controlled later.

source: Chrysikou, Weber & Thompson-Schill (2014) A matched filter hypothesis for cognitive control
finding: Best control level depends on the task. Data-driven tasks (new uses) gain from reduced prefrontal control. Rule-driven tasks gain from it. Idea evaluation returns to frontal control.
numbers: No new data. Cited: inhibitory tDCS over left PFC raised speed and number of creative uses vs right PFC or sham (Chrysikou et al. 2013); eyeblink rate nonlinear for alternative uses, linear for remote associates (Chermahini and Hommel 2010); stroke findings inconsistent (Reverberi 2005 vs de Souza 2010).
limits: First 100,000 of 232,916 characters read. Review without effect sizes. Mixed patient evidence. Inverted-U dopamine means less PFC is not always better.
agent_relevance: Core human basis for O4: relax constraints for open generation, restore them for checking. Choose control level per step.

source: Chrysikou & Thompson-Schill (2011), Limb & Braun (2008) as reported in Chrysikou et al. (2014)
finding: Creative-use generation shows lower prefrontal activity and more visual object-region activity than typical-use generation. Jazz improvisation shows a hypofrontal pattern vs memorised playing.
numbers: No sample sizes in the review text. Reported only qualitatively.
limits: Secondhand through the review. Original studies not opened. Reverse-inference risk from fMRI.
agent_relevance: Origin of the trade-off claim. Hypofrontality evidence is mostly fMRI plus one tDCS line; moderate strength.
